subject: geography
prompt: Geologists define a mineral in a particular way. Which description matches that definition?

image.alt: A cluster of purple mineral crystals on a rock base

options.text: Any rock lying beneath the soil, whatever it is made of
A homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure
A man-made alloy produced by heating metals in a furnace
A mixture of several rocks in fixed proportions

hint: Think of three words: homogenous, natural, structure.
explanation: A mineral is **homogenous** (the same throughout), **naturally occurring** and has a **definable internal structure**. Rocks are combinations of minerals, so calling a rock a mineral confuses the two; alloys are man-made, and a rock is not a fixed mixture. Some rocks, like limestone, consist of just one mineral, but most are made of several in varying proportions.

subject: geography
prompt: Toothpaste, its tube and its brush all depend on minerals or mineral products. Match each use with its source.

image.alt: A paste tube and brush with four mineral names beside them

left.text: Plastic of the tube and the brush

hint: Match the effect first, then the source.
explanation: Fluoride comes from the mineral **fluorite**; titanium oxide, which whitens most pastes, comes from **rutile, ilmenite and anatase**; the sparkle comes from **mica**; and the plastics of the tube and brush are made from **petroleum**. Abrasive minerals such as silica and limestone do the actual cleaning.

subject: geography
prompt: Minerals make up only about 0.3 per cent of what we eat. Which statement explains why they still matter so much?

image.alt: A bar showing 0.3 per cent minerals and 99.7 per cent other nutrients

options.text: They supply 99.7 per cent of the energy we need
They are needed only for bones and teeth, not for life processes
Without them the body could not make use of the other 99.7 per cent of the food
Their share is so small that they can be left out of the diet

hint: The text calls them "potent".
explanation: The chapter says minerals are so potent that without them we **could not utilise the other 99.7 per cent** of foodstuffs, and that life processes cannot occur without them. They do not supply the energy (distractor 1), their role is not limited to bones and teeth, and a small share does not mean a small importance.

subject: geography
prompt: Rock A and Rock B contain the same mineral, shown by the gold dots. Other things being equal, which is more likely to be an **ore** worth mining, and why?

image.alt: Rock A is packed with gold dots; Rock B has only a few

options.text: Rock A, because the mineral is concentrated enough to make extraction commercially viable
Rock B, because a rock with few grains is easier to crush
Both equally, because any rock with the mineral in it is an ore
Neither, because ores are found only in sedimentary rocks

hint: The mineral content must be in sufficient concentration.
explanation: An **ore** is an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements, and its mineral content must be in **sufficient concentration to make extraction commercially viable**. Rock A passes this test; Rock B has too little. Ores are not limited to sedimentary rocks, and not every rock containing the mineral counts as an ore.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **placer deposit**: the sand of a valley floor that holds gold, silver, tin or platinum which water does not corrode.

image.alt: Cross-section of rock layers with a vein, a lode, a coal bed, a weathered layer and valley sands

hint: Look at the valley floor where a stream runs.
explanation: Placer deposits are **alluvial deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills**; they hold minerals not corroded by water, such as gold, silver, tin and platinum. The crack fillings in the hard rock are veins and lodes, the dark band in the layered rock is a coal seam, and the reddish top layer is the weathered residue where bauxite forms.

subject: geography
prompt: Bauxite forms when surface rocks decompose and the soluble parts are removed. Tap the part of the picture where such a **residual mass of weathered material** lies.

image.alt: Cross-section of rock layers with a vein, a lode, a coal bed, a weathered layer and valley sands

hint: It lies at the surface, on top of the hard rock.
explanation: Bauxite is formed by the **decomposition of surface rocks and the removal of soluble constituents**, leaving a residual mass of weathered material that contains the ore. So it lies at the surface, not in a crack (vein or lode), not in a sedimentary bed (coal seam) and not in river sands (placer).

subject: geography
prompt: Coal and some forms of iron ore were concentrated in horizontal layers after long periods under great heat and pressure. Which picture shows minerals occurring in **beds or layers** of sedimentary rock?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: Two crack fillings in hard rock

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A reddish weathered layer on top of rock

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: Sand between two hills with gold grains

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: Horizontal layers of rock with a dark coal band

hint: Look for horizontal strata.
explanation: In **sedimentary rocks** minerals occur in beds or layers formed by deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata. Picture D shows horizontal layers with a coal band. Picture A is veins or lodes (igneous and metamorphic rocks), Picture B is a weathered residue (bauxite) and Picture C is a placer deposit.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each way in which minerals occur with the minerals obtained from it.

image.alt: Cross-section of rock layers showing different ways minerals occur

left.text: Veins and lodes in igneous and metamorphic rocks

hint: Say how each one forms before you pair it.
explanation: Major metallic minerals such as tin, copper, zinc and lead come from **veins and lodes**; coal from **sedimentary beds**; bauxite from **weathered residue**; gold, silver, tin and platinum from **placers**; and common salt, magnesium and bromine from **ocean water**. Tin appears in two lists in the chapter, but the whole set of minerals in each pair tells you which one is meant.

subject: geography
prompt: How are veins and lodes formed in igneous and metamorphic rocks? Put the steps in order.

image.alt: Hot minerals rising through a crack in rock

items.text: Minerals exist in liquid or molten and gaseous forms deep down
They are forced upward through cracks, crevices, faults or joints
Smaller fillings are called veins; larger ones are called lodes
They cool and solidify as they rise

hint: Begin with the state of the minerals.
explanation: Minerals in **liquid/molten and gaseous** form are forced **upward** through cavities towards the surface; they **cool and solidify as they rise**, leaving mineral-filled cracks. The smaller occurrences are **veins** and the larger **lodes**.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these minerals are formed as a result of **evaporation**, especially in arid regions?

image.alt: A shallow pond in a hot dry region shrinking as it dries

options.text: Gypsum
Potash salt
Sodium salt
Bauxite
Tin

hint: They are sedimentary minerals, but not coal or iron ore.
explanation: Another group of sedimentary minerals, **gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt**, forms by evaporation, especially in arid regions. Bauxite forms by weathering of surface rocks, and tin comes from veins/lodes and placer deposits.

subject: geography
prompt: In Jowai and Cherapunjee in Meghalaya, family members dig long, narrow tunnels to take out coal. What is this method called and what has been said about it?

image.alt: A narrow tunnel running sideways into a coal seam under a hillside

options.text: Placer mining, which is nationalised and run by the state
Rat-hole mining, which the National Green Tribunal wants expanded
Quarrying, which needs no permission because families own the minerals
Rat-hole mining, which the National Green Tribunal has declared illegal

hint: It is named after the size of the tunnel.
explanation: Coal mining in Jowai and Cherapunjee is done by families in long narrow tunnels, called **rat-hole mining**. The **National Green Tribunal has declared it illegal** and recommended it be stopped. In most of India minerals are nationalised, but in many tribal areas of the north-east they are owned by individuals or communities.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each setting with what it contains.

image.alt: Four cards: hard old rocks, rock flanks, river plains and dry rock land

left.text: Sedimentary rocks on the flanks of the peninsula, in Gujarat and Assam
Vast alluvial plains of north India

right.text: Most reserves of coal, metallic minerals and mica

hint: Think about the type of rock in each setting.
explanation: Peninsular rocks hold most of the **coal, metallic minerals and mica**; the **sedimentary rocks** on the western and eastern flanks, in Gujarat and in Assam hold most **petroleum**; the **alluvial plains** are almost devoid of economic minerals; Rajasthan has many **non-ferrous** minerals. The differences arise from geological structure, processes and time of formation.

subject: geography
prompt: Which set of factors decides whether a mineral **deposit or reserve** turns into a mine?

image.alt: Three cards: a rock rich in ore, an easy-to-dig tunnel and a shop with a truck

options.text: Colour of the ore, age of the rock and name of the district
The number of minerals identified in the whole world
Concentration of the mineral in the ore, ease of extraction and closeness to the market
Hardness of the mineral alone

hint: Money and distance matter, not looks.
explanation: The concentration of the mineral in the ore, the **ease of extraction** and **closeness to the market** play an important role in economic viability. When a choice among the options is made, a deposit or reserve turns into a mine. Colour, age and the district name do not decide viability.

subject: geography
prompt: Ferrous minerals account for about three-fourths of the value of the production of metallic minerals. If metallic minerals worth ₹ 400 crore were produced in a year, about how much of that value would be ferrous minerals?

image.alt: A bar split into 75 per cent ferrous minerals and 25 per cent others

options.text: ₹ 100 crore
₹ 300 crore
₹ 133 crore
₹ 75 crore

hint: Find three-fourths of 400.
explanation: $\frac{3}{4}\times 400 = 300$, so ferrous minerals account for ₹ 300 crore. ₹ 100 crore is **one**-fourth, ₹ 133 crore comes from **dividing** by 3 instead of taking three-fourths, and ₹ 75 crore wrongly treats "75" as the amount instead of a percentage.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement about magnetite and hematite is correct?

image.alt: Bars: magnetite up to 70 per cent iron, hematite 50 to 60 per cent

options.text: Hematite has up to 70 per cent iron and excellent magnetic qualities
Both have about the same iron content, but only hematite is magnetic
Magnetite is the ore used in the greatest quantity, and hematite is the finest ore
Magnetite has up to 70 per cent iron and is valuable in the electrical industry; hematite has 50-60 per cent and is the ore used in greatest quantity

hint: The finest ore is not the one used the most.
explanation: **Magnetite** is the finest iron ore (up to **70 per cent** iron) with excellent magnetic qualities, valuable in the electrical industry. **Hematite** is the most important industrial ore by quantity used but has a slightly lower iron content (**50-60 per cent**). The distractors swap the two ores or erase the difference.

subject: geography
prompt: In 2018-19, 97 per cent of India's iron ore came from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. If total production had been 200 million tonnes, how many million tonnes came from all other states together?

image.alt: A bar showing 97 per cent from four states and 3 per cent from other states

hint: The other states supplied the remaining 3 per cent.
explanation: The remaining share is $100 - 97 = 3$ per cent, and $\frac{3}{100}\times 200 = 6$ million tonnes. 194 is what the **four states** produced, 3 is the **percentage** not the quantity, and 60 treats 3 per cent as 30 per cent.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each iron ore area with what the chapter says about it.

image.alt: Ore wagons running to a port where a ship waits

left.text: Kudremukh mines in the Western Ghats

right.text: High grade hematite in the Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar districts
14 deposits of super high grade hematite; exported to Japan and South Korea via Visakhapatnam
Ores not of very high quality, but efficiently exploited and exported through Marmagao
A 100 per cent export unit; ore moves as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru

hint: Link the port or the district named in each description.
explanation: Bailadila has **14 deposits of super high grade hematite** exported via **Visakhapatnam**; **Kudremukh** is a **100 per cent export unit** whose slurry travels by pipeline; **Badampahar** (Odisha) has high grade hematite in Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar; the **Goa-Ratnagiri** belt has lower quality ore, exported through **Marmagao**.

subject: geography
prompt: About 10 kg of manganese is needed to make one tonne of steel. How much manganese does a mill need to make 350 tonnes of steel?

image.alt: Steel beams marked 1 tonne beside a sack of manganese marked 10 kg

options.text: 35 kg
350 kg

hint: Multiply the tonnes of steel by the kilograms per tonne.
explanation: $350 \times 10 = 3500$ kg (3.5 tonnes). 35 kg comes from **dividing** 350 by 10, 350 kg uses only 1 kg per tonne, and 35,000 kg adds an extra factor of 10.

subject: geography
prompt: Study the chart of manganese production in 2018-19. Tap the bar of the state with the **second-largest share**.

image.alt: Horizontal bars of the share of manganese production for six producers

hint: Madhya Pradesh is first; find the next longest bar.
explanation: The shares are Madhya Pradesh 33%, **Maharashtra 27%**, Odisha 16%, Karnataka 12%, Andhra Pradesh 10% and others 2%, adding up to 100%. So Maharashtra has the second-largest share.

subject: geography
prompt: In a biogas (gobar gas) plant, put these steps in order.

image.alt: Cross-section of a biogas plant with a feed funnel, a tank, a dome, a stove and a manure pit

items.text: Organic matter decomposes inside the tank
The gas produced is drawn off for cooking and lighting
The leftover slurry is used as improved manure
Cattle dung, farm waste and shrubs are fed into the plant

hint: Decomposition comes before gas.
explanation: Waste is fed in, **decomposition of organic matter yields gas**, which has higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake or charcoal, and the leftover is **better manure**. These are the "twin benefits" to the farmer, and biogas also prevents loss of trees and manure from burning wood and dung cakes.

subject: geography
prompt: A cable maker needs a metal that is malleable, ductile and a good conductor. The chapter names it as mainly used in electrical cables and electronics. Which mineral is it, and how does India stand in it?

image.alt: A coil of copper wire connected to a glowing bulb

options.text: Copper; India has plentiful reserves and exports it
Copper; India is critically deficient in its reserves and production
Bauxite; India is critically deficient in it
Mica; India is critically deficient in it

hint: Malleable, ductile and a good conductor describe a non-ferrous metal.
explanation: **Copper** is malleable, ductile and a good conductor, so it is used in electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries, but India is **critically deficient** in its reserve and production. Bauxite gives aluminium, and mica is valued as an insulator, not a conducting cable metal.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these pairings of a place and its mineral are correct?

image.alt: Cards with iron ore, copper, bauxite and mica

options.text: Khetri mines (Rajasthan): copper
Panchpatmali deposits, Koraput (Odisha): bauxite
Koderma (Jharkhand): mica
Kudremukh (Karnataka): manganese
Neyveli (Tamil Nadu): anthracite

hint: Kudremukh is an iron ore name; Neyveli is a soft coal.
explanation: **Khetri** is a leading copper producer; **Panchpatmali** in Koraput has the most important bauxite deposits of Odisha; **Koderma** (in the Koderma-Gaya-Hazaribagh belt) leads in mica. Kudremukh is an **iron ore** mine, and Neyveli holds **lignite**, a low-grade brown coal, not anthracite.

subject: geography
prompt: Put the working of a tidal power plant in order.

image.alt: A floodgate dam across an inlet with a pipe and turbine

items.text: The tide falls outside the floodgate
At high tide, sea water flows into the inlet
The trapped water flows back to the sea through a pipe that turns a turbine
The floodgate is closed and the water is trapped

hint: The turbine works only after the tide goes out.
explanation: **Floodgate dams** are built across inlets. During high tide water flows in and is trapped when the gate is closed. After the tide falls outside, the retained water flows back to the sea through a pipe carrying it through a **power-generating turbine**.

subject: geography
prompt: Put the steps from rock to metal in order.

image.alt: Bauxite lump and cards for light, strong and conducting uses of aluminium

items.text: Aluminium is obtained later from the alumina
Rocks rich in aluminium silicates decompose
Alumina is obtained from the bauxite
Bauxite, a clay-like substance, is left as deposits

hint: Bauxite comes before alumina, and alumina before the metal.
explanation: Bauxite deposits form by the **decomposition of rocks rich in aluminium silicates**. From the clay-like bauxite, **alumina and later aluminium** are obtained. Aluminium is important because it combines the strength of iron with extreme lightness, good conductivity and great malleability.

subject: geography
prompt: In 2018-19 the five largest limestone-producing states were Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka. Read the chart: what was their combined share of production?

image.alt: Bars for the state shares of limestone production, summing to 100 per cent

options.text: 59 per cent
56 per cent
76 per cent
69 per cent

explanation: $22 + 13 + 13 + 11 + 10 = 69$ per cent. 59 leaves out Karnataka, 56 counts the 13 per cent of Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh only once, and 76 adds Telangana (7 per cent), a sixth state.

subject: geography
prompt: Limestone is found in sedimentary rocks. Which pair of uses is given in the chapter?

image.alt: Iron ore, coal and limestone being loaded into a blast furnace

options.text: Basic raw material for the cement industry and essential for smelting iron ore in a blast furnace
Raw material for fertilisers and insulation of electric cables
Raw material for glass and extraction of aluminium
Raw material for steel alloys and making copper wire

hint: One use is a building material; the other is in making iron.
explanation: Limestone is the **basic raw material for the cement industry** and is **essential for smelting iron ore** in the blast furnace. It occurs with rocks of calcium carbonates or calcium and magnesium carbonates. Insulation is a use of mica, and aluminium comes from bauxite.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Thin plates of mica beside an electric plug

assertion: Mica is one of the most indispensable minerals in the electric and electronic industries.
reason: Mica has excellent di-electric strength, a low power loss factor, insulating properties and resistance to high voltage.
hint: Ask whether the properties explain the use.
explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: mica's **di-electric strength, low power loss, insulating properties and resistance to high voltage** are exactly what electric and electronic industries need. Mica is a non-metallic mineral that splits easily into thin sheets; the Koderma-Gaya-Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand is the leading producer.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statements about the hazards of mining are correct?

image.alt: A mine mouth with dust, fire, fallen rocks and dirty water

options.text: Dust and noxious fumes make miners prone to lung (pulmonary) diseases
Collapsing roofs, flooding and fires in coalmines are constant threats
Mining can contaminate the water sources of the region
Dumping waste and slurry degrades land and soil and pollutes streams and rivers
Mining has no effect on the health of miners
Strict safety rules are the reason mining is called a "killer industry"

hint: Look for the effects on miners and on the environment.
explanation: The first four statements come straight from the chapter. Mining **does** harm miners' health, and it is the **lack** of safety, not strict safety rules, that can make mining a "killer industry": stricter safety regulations and environmental laws are needed to prevent that.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A grid of 100 squares with one square marked for workable deposits

assertion: Mineral resources are finite and non-renewable.
reason: The geological processes of mineral formation are so slow that the rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with the present rate of consumption.
hint: Compare the speed of formation with the speed of use.
explanation: Both are true and R is the reason for A. Workable deposits are only about **one per cent** of the earth's crust, took **millions of years** to form and are being consumed rapidly, so they cannot be replaced in time.

subject: geography
prompt: Which steps does the chapter suggest for conserving mineral resources?

image.alt: Loop of metal goods, scrap metal and new metal

options.text: Recycling of metals
Using scrap metals and other substitutes
Developing technologies that allow low-grade ores to be used at low cost
Extracting the richest deposits as fast as possible while they last
Using mineral resources in a planned and sustainable manner
Ignoring depth and quality, since extraction costs do not change

hint: Think "reuse, replace, plan".
explanation: The chapter calls for **planned and sustainable use**, **improved technologies for low-grade ores**, **recycling of metals** and **scrap and substitutes**. Rushing to use rich deposits wastes a short-lived resource, and costs actually **rise** as extraction goes deeper and quality falls.

subject: geography
prompt: Which picture shows a **non-conventional** source of energy?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A heap of coal

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A pile of firewood logs

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A wind turbine turning

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A fuel pump

hint: Conventional sources are the old, familiar ones such as fuels burnt for heat.
explanation: Wind is a **non-conventional** source, like solar, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy. **Firewood, coal, petroleum** (from the fuel pump), natural gas and electricity are conventional sources.

subject: geography
prompt: More than 70 per cent of the energy needed in rural households comes from firewood and cattle dung cake. Why is the use of dung cake being discouraged?

image.alt: A bar showing more than 70 per cent of rural energy from firewood and dung cake

options.text: It gives more heat than biogas but costs more
It is a fossil fuel whose mining harms miners
It is a non-conventional source that is hard to obtain
Burning it uses up valuable manure that could be put on farms

hint: Think of what the farmer loses.
explanation: Using dung cake **consumes valuable manure** that could be used in agriculture, and using firewood is getting harder as forest area decreases. Dung cake and firewood are conventional, not fossil fuels, and biogas, which also gives manure, has a higher thermal efficiency than dung cake.

subject: geography
prompt: Put the formation and grading of coal in order, from the plant material to the best quality.

image.alt: Plants in a swamp buried under layers that press them into coal

items.text: Anthracite, the highest quality hard coal, is formed
Decaying plants in swamps form peat
Deep burial at higher temperatures gives bituminous coal
Peat is changed into soft brown lignite

hint: The deeper and hotter, the better the coal.
explanation: Coal is formed by the **compression of plant material over millions of years**; its form depends on compression, depth and time of burial. **Peat** has low carbon and high moisture; **lignite** is a low-grade brown coal; **bituminous** is the most popular in commercial use; **anthracite** is the highest quality hard coal.

subject: geography
prompt: A steel plant needs coal with a special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces. Which should it choose?

image.alt: Four lumps labelled peat, lignite, bituminous and anthracite

options.text: Metallurgical coal, a high-grade bituminous coal
Anthracite, because it is the highest quality hard coal
Lignite from Neyveli, because it is soft with high moisture
Peat, because it forms first in swamps

hint: It is a grade of the most popular commercial coal.
explanation: **Metallurgical coal** is high-grade bituminous coal with special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces. Anthracite is the highest quality but is not named for this use. Lignite (low-grade, high moisture) is used to generate electricity, and peat has low carbon and low heating capacity.

subject: geography
prompt: Coal in the north-eastern states of Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland belongs to which series?

image.alt: Bars: Gondwana coal a little over 200 million years, Tertiary coal about 55 million

options.text: Gondwana deposits, a little over 200 million years old
Tertiary deposits, only about 55 million years old
Gondwana deposits, about 55 million years old
Tertiary deposits, a little over 200 million years old

hint: The major metallurgical coal of the Damodar valley is the other series.
explanation: North-eastern coal is **Tertiary**, about **55 million years** old. The major resources of **Gondwana** coal (a little over 200 million years old, and metallurgical) lie in the Damodar valley, with Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro as important coalfields. The wrong options mix up the series or their ages.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A coalfield with a mine and a power station next to it

assertion: Heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near the coalfields.
reason: Coal gains weight when it is burnt.
hint: Check what happens to the weight of coal when it is used.
explanation: A is true: coal is a **bulky material**, so it is cheaper to set up industries near the coalfields. R is false: coal **loses weight** on use because it is reduced to ash. The false reason is what makes this a choice (c) rather than (a).

subject: geography
prompt: Petroleum collects in a porous layer that is sealed in by non-porous layers. Tap the **non-porous layer above the oil-bearing rock** that stops the oil from rising any further.

image.alt: Cross-section of an upfold of rock layers with gas, oil and water in the porous layer and a well

hint: It lies on top of the arch of the porous layer.
explanation: In an **anticline (upfold)**, oil is trapped in the crest of the porous limestone or sandstone layer, and **non-porous layers** keep it from rising or sinking. **Gas, being lighter, occurs above the oil.**

subject: geography
prompt: Most petroleum in India occurs in anticlines and fault traps in tertiary rocks. Which picture shows oil trapped at the crest of an **upfold**?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: Flat layers with oil seeping upward

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: An arch of rock layers with oil held at the top under a cap

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: Cracks in hard rock filled with mineral

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: Sand on a valley floor with gold grains

hint: The oil must be held in by a cover on top.
explanation: Picture B shows an arch (anticline) with a porous layer capped by a non-porous layer, so oil collects at the crest. In Picture A the flat layers have no trap, Picture C shows veins of metallic minerals and Picture D a placer deposit.

subject: geography
prompt: Why are petroleum refineries called a "nodal industry"?

image.alt: A refinery tower linked to four other industries

options.text: They stand at the junctions of gas pipelines
They produce coal for thermal power stations
They supply raw materials to synthetic textile, fertiliser and many chemical industries
They turn natural gas into electricity for homes

hint: A node is a centre that many things connect to.
explanation: Petroleum refineries act as a **nodal industry** because they provide raw material for the **synthetic textile, fertiliser and numerous chemical industries**. Petroleum also gives fuel for heat and lighting and lubricants for machinery.

subject: geography
prompt: The first Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur pipeline was 1,700 km long. India's cross-country gas pipelines have since grown to 18,500 km and are expected to reach over 34,000 km as a Gas Grid. How many more kilometres are needed to reach 34,000 km from today's length?

image.alt: Bars for 1,700 km, 18,500 km and 34,000 km of pipelines

hint: Start from the present length, not from the first pipeline.
explanation: $34000 - 18500 = 15500$ km. 32,300 km starts from the first 1,700 km pipeline, 16,800 km is the growth already achieved ($18500 - 1700$), and 52,500 km **adds** the two lengths.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Four lumps labelled peat, lignite, bituminous and anthracite

assertion: Peat is the highest quality coal.
reason: Peat has low carbon and high moisture content and a low heating capacity.
hint: Is low carbon a sign of high quality?
explanation: A is false: **peat** is the first stage, formed by decaying plants in swamps, while **anthracite** is the highest quality hard coal. R is true, since peat has low carbon, high moisture and low heating capacity, which is why peat is a poor fuel, not a top one.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Falling water on a turbine beside a flame under a boiler

assertion: Hydro electricity is generated from a renewable resource.
reason: Thermal power stations burn coal, petroleum and natural gas to drive turbines.
hint: Does the reason say anything about why water is renewable?
explanation: Both are true. Hydro electricity comes from **fast-flowing water, a renewable resource**, and thermal stations burn coal, petroleum and natural gas. But R describes thermal power; it does not explain why hydro power is renewable, so the answer is (b). Once generated, the electricity is exactly the same.

subject: geography
prompt: In this thermal power station, tap the part where steam spins blades to drive the generator: the **turbine**.

image.alt: Schematic of coal heap, boiler, chimney, turbine, generator and power line

hint: Steam flows from the boiler into it.
explanation: In thermal power, coal, petroleum or natural gas is burnt to make **steam that drives turbines**, which in turn run the generator. The boiler makes the steam, the chimney carries smoke away, and the generator makes the electricity.

subject: geography
prompt: Hydro electricity uses fast-flowing water to drive turbines. Tap the **pipe that carries water from the reservoir to the turbine**.

image.alt: Cross-section of a dam with a power house and a river below

hint: It runs through the base of the dam.
explanation: Water from the reservoir rushes down a **pipe through the dam** to the turbine; the turbine turns the generator. Multi-purpose projects like Bhakra Nangal, Damodar Valley and Kopili produce hydroelectric power this way.

subject: geography
prompt: Atomic (nuclear) energy is obtained by altering the structure of atoms. Which minerals are used, and what is the Monazite sand of Kerala rich in?

image.alt: A split atom giving heat that makes steam to turn a turbine and light a bulb

options.text: Uranium and petroleum; Monazite sands are rich in oil
Uranium and thorium; Monazite sands are rich in thorium
Thorium and copper; Monazite sands are rich in uranium
Uranium and thorium; Monazite sands are rich in uranium

hint: Both minerals are named, but Monazite is linked to only one.
explanation: **Uranium and thorium** (found in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan) are used for atomic power. The **Monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium**. Altering the atoms releases much energy as heat, which is used to generate electric power.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the **floodgate** that is closed at high tide so the sea water stays trapped in the inlet.

image.alt: Side view of a floodgate dam across a sea inlet with a pipe and turbine

hint: It sits in the wall that separates the sea from the inlet.
explanation: A **floodgate dam** across an inlet traps water at high tide when the gate is closed. When the tide falls, the trapped water flows back to the sea through a pipe and a turbine. The Gulf of Khambhat, the Gulf of Kuchchh and the Sunderban delta are ideal sites.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the part of the biogas plant where the **gas collects** before it is piped to the stove.

image.alt: Cross-section of a village biogas plant

spots.label: Feeding funnel for dung and waste

hint: It sits above the ground and has a pipe from its top.
explanation: Gas given off by the decomposing slurry rises into the **dome** and is piped to the stove. The slurry stays in the digester tank and then flows out as improved manure. Plants using cattle dung are called **gobar gas plants** and give twin benefits: energy and better manure.

subject: geography
prompt: Groundwater heated by hot rocks rises to the surface as **steam** to drive turbines. Tap that rising steam.

image.alt: Cross-section with hot rock below, groundwater, a steam channel and a turbine house

hint: It is the white column going up from the hot zone.
explanation: The Earth grows hotter with depth. Where the geothermal gradient is high, groundwater absorbs heat from rocks and **turns to steam when it rises**; the steam drives turbines. Two experimental projects in India are at Manikaran (Parvati valley, Himachal Pradesh) and Puga Valley, Ladakh.
